<h1 class="hero-title">OTTO <em>Lab</em></h1>
<p class="hero-descriptor">Observational Target Trial Operations</p>

<p class="hero-lede">How do we study cause and effect in psychology when we can't run an experiment? We specify the randomised trial we <em>would</em> run if we could, the <em>target trial</em>, and emulate it using longitudinal data.</p>
<div class="hero-actions">
<a href="research.qmd" class="btn btn-primary">Research</a>
<a href="resources.qmd" class="btn btn-secondary">Resources</a>
<a href="mailto:joseph.bulbulia@vuw.ac.nz" class="btn btn-secondary">Email Joseph Bulbulia</a>
</div>
<p class="hero-text">Causal inference from observational data requires assumptions. One of these is the assumption of no unmeasured confounding, also called the exchangeability assumption. To treat an observed assignment as "as good as random", there must be no residual association between the treatment and potential outcome after we have included a set of measured covariates. Because this assumption cannot be tested, we run sensitivity analyses.</p>

## Why causal inference?

Having yellow fingers predicts lung cancer but does not cause it. A smoker who scrubs their fingers to remove the stains will not reduce their risk. Similarly, ice cream consumption predicts shark attacks but does not cause them. Sunshine causes people both to seek the refreshing snack and to seek out the beaches where shark attacks occur.

Despite the ubiquity of "predict" language, most psychological scientists are interested in causality.

::: {#fig-otto layout-ncol=2}

![*a* = 0: ball not in mouth](images/ottos/web/otto-dog-ball.jpg){fig-alt="A dog rears up on his hind legs in silhouette against a setting sun, jaws open as a ball hovers just above his snout."}

![*a* = 1: ball in mouth](images/ottos/web/otto-dog-no-ball.jpg){fig-alt="A dog leaps in a misty field at dusk, in silhouette, with a ball held in his mouth."}

Left: ball not in mouth (*a* = 0). Right: ball in mouth (*a* = 1; look closely). At any one moment we can observe Otto under only one of the two conditions; the other is counterfactual. Most of what the lab does follows from that inconvenience.
:::

## `religionmap.org`

When we're not doing causal inference, we maintain [`religionmap.org`](https://religionmap.org/), which maps places of worship worldwide for spatial and cultural research.

[Visit `religionmap.org`](https://religionmap.org/) · [Code](https://github.com/go-bayes/places-of-worship)

## Collaboration and teaching

We welcome MA and PhD students interested in causal inference, longitudinal methods, religion, or social psychology, and we collaborate with researchers in New Zealand and abroad. We also teach causal inference and maintain open-source R packages including [`margot`](resources.qmd#r-packages) and [`boilerplate`](research.qmd#software). To discuss supervision or collaboration, email Joseph Bulbulia at [joseph.bulbulia@vuw.ac.nz](mailto:joseph.bulbulia@vuw.ac.nz). You can also meet our [inspiring Ottos](team.qmd#the-ottos).
